newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour leaders appeal for unity.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour leaders appeal for unity.

text.p: Leaders of Britain's Labour Party appealed on Saturday for unity ahead of their last annual conference before general elections in which they are tipped to regain power after 17 years in opposition.
Party leader Tony Blair, who has sought to modernise the party and win the political middle ground, said he wanted the conference to show that Labour's changes were "real and lasting".

"I am confident that if this week goes well for us -- if we are united in our purpose, clear about our direction and sure in the policies we put forward -- we can send the Tories (Conservatives) into a tailspin," he said in a speech prepared for delivery at a youth conference.

"This conference gives us the chance to show that the changes we have made are real and lasting, that the party is united around a core vision and our policies will make that vision a reality," Blair added.
But differences on the pace of change and some of Labour's new policies were evident even before the conference got underway in the northern town of Blackpool on Monday.
In an interview with The Times, published on Saturday, deputy leader John Prescott said he admired and respected Blair but expressed unease about the headlong pace of party reform.
"Tony's very strongly of the view that you just don't stop. He wants to keep the party adjusting. I think he's right about that. The real problem is: how far do you go without derailing?
"Sometimes you can go too fast. It will hit the bloody wall, the buffers. The more and more you pile on the change, the more and more people feel a little uneasy," Prescott was quoted as saying.
Blair has ditched his party's long-standing commitment to nationalisation of major industries and seeing to re-evaluate Labour's traditionally close relationship with trade unions.
Labour now enjoys a 20 point lead over the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls just eight months before Britain must hold general elections.
The leadership is expected to come under attack at the conference from left-wingers over workers' rights and pensions.
Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown made his own appeal for party discipline in an interview published on Saturday in the parliamentary House Magazine.
"Labour has got to prove to the electorate that it is disciplined and that it will take the task of government seriously," Brown said.
"I hope that we will operate as a disciplined parliamentary party over these next few months in the spirit that the party wants us to," he added.
The Blackpool conference is expected to be the battleground for a campaign spearheaded by former cabinet minister Barbara Castle to restore a link between the state pension and average earnings.
But Labour, fearful of being tagged by the Conservatives as taxers and spenders, wants instead to provide the 700,000 neediest pensioners with a top-up to their pension entitlement.
Castle, 85, said she wanted Blair to win the election but warned that his rush to capture the middle ground could backfire.

"What's happening is that we're becoming more and more indistinguishable from the Tories (Conservatives). And if you think that's the way to win the election, I think it's a gross mis-estimate of what's happening.
"And remember, I've been through every general election since the war...I've seen the tactics fail," Castle said.
